$comment:
The repository settings that are NOT code — branch rules, merge policy and deployment environments — written down because nothing else can hold them. A clone carries every gate in this tree, and none of these: delete the repository and they are gone, recreate it and they come back as GitHub's defaults, which are not these. That is the failure this file exists to prevent, and it is not hypothetical — `ci-gate` and `analysis-gate` being required checks is the only thing standing between a red run and a merge.

Apply it with `gh api --method PATCH repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity --input <the repository object>`, `gh api --method POST repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity/rulesets --input <a rulesets entry>`, and `gh api --method PUT repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity/environments/production --input <an environments entry>`, once `main` exists: ruleset conditions name `~DEFAULT_BRANCH`, which does not resolve until the first push, so the ruleset is created after the branch. Read the live state back with `GET /repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity/rulesets` and `GET /repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity/environments` to diff it against this file.

METHOD MATTERS, and getting it wrong is quiet. `PUT /repos/{owner}/{repo}` — the verb this file instructed until it was applied and answered — returns **404**, not 405: the request reaches authorization, then GitHub reports Not Found. A reader who runs it concludes the manifest is wrong about the repository's identity, rather than that the verb was. The correct verb is **PATCH**, which is what GitHub's own endpoint is called. An environment's request body takes `reviewers`, `prevent_self_review`, `wait_timer` and `deployment_branch_policy`; it does **not** take `name` or `protection_rules`, both of which are response-only fields and fail with a 422 naming the offending key.

This is a record, not an enforcer: no gate compares it to reality, because doing so needs an admin token this repository's sessions do not hold. Check it by hand when something about landing a change feels different from what is written here.

EVERY entry under `environments` here is live today. An entry that is not applied is worse than no entry: GitHub creates an environment implicitly the first time a job declares one that does not exist, with no protection rules at all, so the file would describe a gate while the runner runs the job straight through. Verify with `GET /repos/ecoma-io/ecoma-identity/environments` before assuming an entry took.

The tier-by-tier derivation behind each rule — Scorecard's `Branch-Protection` check, what every rule buys and what it deliberately forfeits, and why `required_linear_history` is absent — lives in `ecoma`'s `.github/repository-settings.json` and is not restated here. The shape and the parameters below are identical to `runtime-trail`'s; only the two differences are called out in this file.

repository.$comment: Merge policy. Exactly one method stays enabled, so the strategy is a mechanism rather than whichever button someone clicked. `allow_auto_merge` is on because the merge queue below rides on it: with the queue required on `main`, enabling auto-merge is how a pull request enters the queue, through the API and the UI alike — without it the queue is declared but unenterable. `delete_branch_on_merge` is safe under merge commits and only under them: a merge commit's second parent puts a branch's commits on `main` as the same objects, so deleting the ref removes a pointer and not history.

rules.$comment:
Mirrors `ecoma` and `runtime-trail` exactly. `required_linear_history` is deliberately ABSENT: it forbids merge commits outright, and linearity is recoverable as a view (`git log --first-first-parent`) while the pull-request boundary a merge commit records is not recoverable once a rebase has flattened it — that boundary is what makes `git revert -m 1 <merge>` the one operation this repository's charter promises.

`required_approving_review_count: 0` with `require_last_push_approval: false` and `dismiss_stale_reviews_on_push: false` is not an oversight and must not be raised one at a time: this is a single-maintainer repository, and GitHub defines last-push approval as an approval from someone other than the person who pushed. Raising either boolean alone buys nothing, because the tier holding it stays gated behind the approval count. All three move together, and only when a second maintainer exists.

`require_extra_approval_for_unattributed_changes: true` is GitHub's own default for this rule and was returned by the API rather than sent by this file; it is written down here so the diff against live state is empty rather than one-directional. It requires a fresh approval when new commits land that nobody has authored an attribution for — meaningless in a repository where every commit is signed, which is why it costs nothing.

`integration_id` 15368 is GitHub Actions: it pins each check to the app that produces it, so a differently-owned check of the same name cannot satisfy it. `ci-gate` and `analysis-gate` are single aggregating jobs on purpose — one name to require, so adding a CI job never means remembering to add it here too. A repository that adds a third required job must add it to this file in the same commit; the failure mode is a merge queue that sits on a check the repository no longer requires, or a red run that cannot block a merge.

Every pull request lands here. No direct merges and no direct pushes to `main`. The `identity` production canary's two human gates are a separate mechanism — GitHub *environments* with required reviewers — because a workflow-level `if:` can be removed by anyone who can push a workflow file, while an environment's required reviewers cannot.

environments.$comment:
The `production` environment, and the only one declared here because it is the only one that gates anything. Six jobs carry `environment: production` — `.github/workflows/deploy-production.yml:125,192,224,260` and `.github/workflows/deploy-worker.yml:1614,1768`. ADR-0014's whole mechanical point is that this gate lives HERE rather than in a workflow `if:`: a workflow-level condition can be edited by the same pull request that would benefit from editing it, while an environment's protection rules are repository settings a pull request cannot change.

WITHOUT this entry the gate does not degrade, it does not exist. GitHub creates an environment implicitly the first time a job declares one that does not exist, with no protection rules at all, and the job runs straight through. Four workflow comments describe an approval that is never requested — the exact failure `AGENTS.md` names first: describing unimplemented behaviour as though it works.

`reviewers` names johnitvn, who is also the person who pushes, and `prevent_self_review: true` forbids them from approving it. That combination is DELIBERATE and the alternative is worse. Without `prevent_self_review` the single named reviewer can approve their own deployment and the gate is a rubber stamp that reads like a control. With it, the deployment waits for somebody who is not the author — so the first production promotion in this repository will sit at `Waiting for approval` until a second person is added as a collaborator and a reviewer. That is the correct outcome for a gate whose entire purpose is a second pair of eyes, and it is stated here rather than discovered later at 50% of production traffic.

The job is NOT blocked while it waits; it sits in `Waiting for approval` and a maintainer approves it from the run's deployment page. Read the docs before changing `reviewers` or `prevent_self_review` — see `$comment_reviewer_id` below for the one non-obvious part.
environments.name: production
environments.$comment_reviewer_id:
Reviewers are written as `{"type": "User", "id": <numeric user id>}` — an APP installation id, not a login. johnitvn is id 8359652; look it up with `gh api user --jq .id` while logged in as that account, or `GET /users/johnitvn`. Writing a login string here is rejected, and so is a numeric id that is not a real user id — both fail with a 422 rather than creating an environment with no protection, which is the good failure mode.

When a second maintainer is added, add them to `reviewers` (GitHub accepts up to six) and consider `prevent_self_review: false`, which lets the author approve once a second reviewer exists. Do both in one change; either alone is weaker than it reads.
environments.$comment_branches: `deployment_branch_policy: null` means no deployment-branch restriction: any ref may deploy to `production`. Restricting it to protected branches would REFUSE the deployments this environment exists to gate, because a promotion runs from a tag-triggered workflow, not from a branch, and tags are not branches. The gate here is the reviewer, not the ref — and a version id reaches a promotion job only from `build_and_upload`, which runs only on a release tag.
